title: Also, is not, right?
titleJp: わたしも ブラジルじんですよ
canDo: I can say that something is also true of another person or thing, by swapping は for も.
I can make a noun sentence negative (〜じゃないです) and answer いいえ with the negative sentence plus the correct information.
I can recognize じゃありません as the more formal version of the negative.
I can use ね to ask for agreement ("…, right?") and よ to give new information ("…, you know").

blocks.t: Warm-up: point at 3 objects and say what they are and how much they cost (lessons 02-1 and 02-2)
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each word and repeat it twice
Grammar: the 3 points, each with its examples read aloud and one 🔬
Block 6: the Lesson 2 video, pausing on the sentence endings, or the Sakubi sections as a second explanation
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + write your questions in the lesson notebook

skills: Building X は Y です and answering はい、そうです。 (lesson 01-1).
Pointing at things and places with これ/この/ここ (lesson 02-1).

vocab.en: also, too (takes the place of は)
is not / am not / are not
is not / am not / are not (more formal)
that's not so, that's not it

grammar.title: N も
grammar.explanation:
も means **"also / too"** and **takes the place of は**: the sentence stays the same, only は becomes も. マリアさんは ブラジルじんです。 → ルーカスさんも ブラジルじんです。 ("Lucas is Brazilian too.")
• も is an **inclusion** label: it adds its block to something already said ("Maria is Brazilian — and Lucas is included"). It sticks to **the block that is "also"**, not to the end of the sentence like English "too". The PREDICATE (…です) is the same as in the sentence before; that's exactly why you use も.
• は and も never go together: わたしはも ✗. In lesson 04-3 you'll see that も also takes the place of が and を, while with other particles, such as に and で, it goes after them instead.
• In a question: すずきさんも いしゃですか。 ("Is Mr./Ms. Suzuki a doctor too?")
• If the predicate changes, go back to は: ペドロさんは がくせいです。アナさんは かいしゃいんです。
• With the negative (point 4b), も means "not … either".
grammar.structure: [A] は X です。 [B] も X です。

examples.jp: マリアさんは ブラジルじんです。ルーカスさんも ブラジルじんです。
examples.kana: マリアさんは ブラジルじんです。ルーカスさんも ブラジルじんです。
examples.romaji: Maria-san wa burajirujin desu. Rūkasu-san mo burajirujin desu.
examples.en: Maria is Brazilian. Lucas is Brazilian too.

examples.jp: たなかさんは いしゃです。すずきさんも いしゃですか。
examples.kana: たなかさんは いしゃです。すずきさんも いしゃですか。
examples.romaji: Tanaka-san wa isha desu. Suzuki-san mo isha desu ka.
examples.en: Mr./Ms. Tanaka is a doctor. Is Mr./Ms. Suzuki a doctor too?

examples.jp: この とけいは いちまんえんです。その とけいも いちまんえんです。
examples.kana: この とけいは いちまんえんです。その とけいも いちまんえんです。
examples.romaji: Kono tokei wa ichiman en desu. Sono tokei mo ichiman en desu.
examples.en: This watch is 10,000 yen. That watch (near you) is 10,000 yen too.

pitfalls: は and も don't combine: わたしはも ✗ → わたしも ✓. も replaces は.
も goes right after the thing that is "also", not at the end of the sentence like English "too": わたしは ブラジルじんですも ✗ → わたしも ブラジルじんです ✓ ("I'm Brazilian too").
Only use も when the PREDICATE repeats. If it changes, it's は: アナさんは がくせいです。ペドロさんも かいしゃいんです ✗ → ペドロさんは かいしゃいんです ✓.
howToStudy: Say 3 pairs of sentences out loud about you and someone else: わたしは 〜です。(name)さんも 〜です。
Tap 🔬 on example 1: in both sentences the PREDICATE is the same (ブラジルじんです). マリアさんは shows up as the TOPIC and ルーカスさんも as ALSO: only the first block changes.
In your notebook, write 3 sentences with は and, under each one, the version with も for another person or thing.

grammar.title: N じゃないです
grammar.explanation:
To make a noun sentence negative, swap **です** for **じゃないです**: がくせいです → がくせいじゃないです ("I'm not a student"). Nothing else changes: the TOPIC still takes は, and the negative sits **at the end**, inside the PREDICATE. That's why it matters so much to read to the end: English tells you "not" early ("I am **not**…"), but in Japanese you only find out whether it's yes or no in the last block.
• **じゃありません** means the same thing and is the **more formal** version.
• Where the pieces come from: じゃ is the spoken contraction of **では**, and ない means "not"; です keeps it polite. That's why formal writing uses the uncontracted ではありません.
• Now you can answer "no" in full, as promised in lesson 01-1: いいえ、にほんじんじゃないです。ブラジルじんです。
• A short answer: いいえ、そうじゃないです。 ("No, that's not so.")
• With も, it becomes "not … either": ペドロさんも にほんじんじゃないです。
• For now, じゃないです is for nouns. Verbs and い-adjectives make their negatives differently (lessons 03-1 and 05-1).
• Going further (Sakubi): without です, じゃない is the casual "isn't" — the negative of だ (lesson 08-1) — and you'll hear it a lot in games. Said with a rising voice, 〜じゃない？ can also mean "isn't it?", asking the other person to confirm, so listen to the tone.
grammar.structure: [X] は [N] じゃないです。 · more formal: [X] は [N] じゃありません。

examples.jp: ルーカスさんは にほんじんじゃないです。ブラジルじんです。
examples.kana: ルーカスさんは にほんじんじゃないです。ブラジルじんです。
examples.romaji: Rūkasu-san wa nihonjin ja nai desu. Burajirujin desu.

examples.jp: それは わたしの かさじゃないです。
examples.kana: それは わたしの かさじゃないです。
examples.romaji: Sore wa watashi no kasa ja nai desu.

examples.jp: やまださんは がくせいですか。— いいえ、がくせいじゃありません。かいしゃいんです。
examples.kana: やまださんは がくせいですか。— いいえ、がくせいじゃありません。かいしゃいんです。
examples.romaji: Yamada-san wa gakusei desu ka. — Iie, gakusei ja arimasen. Kaishain desu.
examples.en: Is Ms. Yamada a student? — No, she isn't a student. She's an office worker.

pitfalls: The negative is at the end. In がくせい…じゃないです, don't decide the meaning before you've read the last block.
English puts "not" early ("I am not a student"). Japanese puts it at the very end: わたしは じゃない がくせいです ✗ → わたしは がくせいじゃないです ✓.
じゃないです replaces the whole です: がくせいですじゃない ✗ → がくせいじゃないです ✓.
For now, ask in the affirmative (がくせいですか。). Negative questions (〜じゃないですか) have a different meaning and come later.
howToStudy: Say out loud 5 things you are NOT (にほんじんじゃないです。せんせいじゃないです。…) and, after each one, what you are.
Tap 🔬 on example 3 and compare the PREDICATE of the question (がくせいですか) with the one in the answer (がくせいじゃありません). いいえ shows up as an INTERJECTION, outside the sentence.
In your notebook, make the sentences from the lesson 01-1 homework negative, first with じゃないです and then with じゃありません.

grammar.title: 〜ね / 〜よ
grammar.explanation:
ね and よ come **after です**, at the very end, and don't change the content of the sentence: they change **the tone**, showing what you think the other person already knows. The descriptions below are a guide, not exact rules: these endings are learned mostly **by ear**, by hearing them again and again.
• **ね** = "…, right?", "…, isn't it?": you expect the other person to **agree** or to confirm something you both see or know. Both of you are eating: この とんかつは おいしいですね。
• **よ** = "…, you know", "I'm telling you": you're giving **new information** the other person doesn't have.
• そうですね = "that's right", agreeing. It also buys time, like English "let me see…".
• You'll often hear **よね** together, checking something you think you know ("…, isn't it?").
• At the start of a sentence, ね (or ねえ) just gets someone's attention, like "hey" — among friends.
• おいしい ("delicious") and たかい ("expensive") are adjectives; they come in lesson 05-1, but you can already use おいしいです and たかいです.
• Going further (Sakubi): casual speech has more of these endings — な (emphasis, often said to yourself), ぞ and ぜ (assertive, and they sound masculine), わ and さ. You'll meet them in games and manga: learn to recognize them, but don't use them yet.

examples.jp: ペドロさんは ブラジルじんですね。— ええ、そうです。
examples.kana: ペドロさんは ブラジルじんですね。— ええ、そうです。
examples.romaji: Pedoro-san wa burajirujin desu ne. — Ē, sō desu.
examples.en: Pedro, you're Brazilian, right? — Yes, that's right. [lit. Pedro is Brazilian, right?]

examples.jp: あの ひとは にほんごの せんせいですよ。
examples.kana: あの ひとは にほんごの せんせいですよ。
examples.romaji: Ano hito wa nihongo no sensei desu yo.
examples.en: That person over there is the Japanese teacher, you know.

examples.jp: この かばんは たかいですね。— ええ、にまんえんですよ。
examples.kana: この かばんは たかいですね。— ええ、にまんえんですよ。
examples.romaji: Kono kaban wa takai desu ne. — Ē, niman en desu yo.
examples.en: This bag is expensive, isn't it? — Yes, it's 20,000 yen, you know.

pitfalls: Don't use ね for something the other person can't know yet. わたしの なまえは ペドロですね ✗ sounds as if they should already know your name. In an introduction, add nothing: わたしの なまえは ペドロです ✓.
Too much よ sounds pushy, as if you were correcting the other person all the time. With teachers and bosses, use it sparingly.
ね asks for confirmation of something you already think (ブラジルじんですね = "you're Brazilian, right?"). If you really don't know the answer, ask with か: ブラジルじんですか ✓.
ね and よ always come last, after です: ブラジルじんねです ✗ → ブラジルじんですね ✓.
howToStudy: Look at photos on your phone and comment on them out loud with ね, as if someone were looking with you: 〜さんですね。, おいしいですね。
Make up 3 "tips" for a friend with よ: あの きっさてんは たかいですよ。

Tap 🔊 on the examples and repeat, copying the tone of each ending. Then tap 🔬 on example 3: ね and よ stay at the end of the PREDICATE block, and tapping that block explains what the ending adds — the content doesn't change.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook, writing the Japanese in kana. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day.

tasks.prompt: Make each sentence negative with じゃないです. Then read each one aloud again, this time with じゃありません.

items.q: わたしは にほんじんです。

a.jp: わたしは にほんじんじゃないです。
a.romaji: Watashi wa nihonjin ja nai desu.

items.note: More formal: わたしは にほんじんじゃありません。

items.q: これは わたしの ぼうしです。

a.jp: これは わたしの ぼうしじゃないです。
a.romaji: Kore wa watashi no bōshi ja nai desu.

items.q: ここは としょかんです。

a.jp: ここは としょかんじゃないです。
a.romaji: Koko wa toshokan ja nai desu.

items.q: アナさんは かいしゃいんです。

a.jp: アナさんは かいしゃいんじゃないです。
a.romaji: Ana-san wa kaishain ja nai desu.

items.q: その かさは ごひゃくえんです。

a.jp: その かさは ごひゃくえんじゃないです。
a.romaji: Sono kasa wa gohyaku en ja nai desu.

items.note: A price is a noun too: the negative works the same way.

tasks.prompt: Fill in は or も.

items.q: マリアさんは がくせいです。アナさん＿ がくせいです。
たなかさんは にほんじんです。ルーカスさん＿ ブラジルじんです。
この じしょは にせんえんです。その じしょ＿ にせんえんです。
わたしは いしゃじゃないです。ペドロさん＿ いしゃじゃないです。
ここは としょかんです。あそこ＿ ゆうびんきょくです。
items.note: The predicate changes (としょかん × ゆうびんきょく): は.

tasks.prompt: ね or よ? Choose, and tell yourself why.

items.q: You're both eating and the food is great: おいしいです＿。
items.note: You both know it: seeking agreement.

items.q: Your friend doesn't know who that person is, and you do: あの ひとは すずきさんです＿。
You think your classmate is Brazilian and want to check: ブラジルじんです＿。
items.note: Checking: ね. ブラジルじんですよね。 ("you're Brazilian, aren't you?") is also correct.

items.q: Your friend thinks the watch is cheap, but you know it's expensive: たかいです＿。
items.note: You're telling your friend something they don't know.

tasks.prompt: Write 5 or 6 sentences comparing yourself with a friend: at least 2 with も, 2 with じゃないです and 1 with ね or よ. Then read them aloud.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: わたしは ブラジルじんです。ともだちの ルーカスさんも ブラジルじんです。わたしは せんせいじゃないです。かいしゃいんです。ルーカスさんも せんせいじゃないです。いしゃですよ。
a.romaji: Watashi wa burajirujin desu. Tomodachi no Rūkasu-san mo burajirujin desu. Watashi wa sensei ja nai desu. Kaishain desu. Rūkasu-san mo sensei ja nai desu. Isha desu yo.
a.en: I'm Brazilian. My friend Lucas is Brazilian too. I'm not a teacher. I'm an office worker. Lucas isn't a teacher either. He's a doctor, you know.

items.note: Check: も in place of は when the predicate repeats, じゃないです at the end, and よ only for new information.

workbook.tip: Do it at the end of the lesson: it covers all of Lesson 2. Answer in full sentences.
You need the official Genki audio. Do it last and check it with the official Genki Answer Key.

practice.what: Play normally and hunt for sentence endings: ね, よ and negatives (the game may use the casual form じゃない, without です), plus も in the middle of a sentence. Each time, say out loud what it does: agreement, new information, negative or "also". Copy 2 of those lines into your notebook and save 1 in the app's Mining, with every word looked up in a dictionary. Other endings (な, ぞ, さ…) may show up too: just note them.
Drills → Particles: 10 min, paying attention to は × も. Then clear today's reviews (🌊 All), including the Lesson 2 vocabulary and the sentences you have mined.
Journal: write 3 sentences about you and a friend with も and じゃないです, then open "Anatomy of what I wrote".
Tap 🔊 on each example in this lesson and repeat along 3 times, copying the tone of ね and よ.
Record 1 minute about you and a friend using も, じゃないです, ね and よ (use homework h4 as a script).

culture.title: あいづち: showing you're listening
culture.body: In Japanese, the listener usually gives **short, frequent signals** while the other person talks: はい, ええ, うん (among friends), そうですか, そうですね, へえ (surprise), often with a slight nod. These signals are called あいづち, and they generally mean "I'm following you", **not necessarily "I agree"**: a はい in the middle of someone's sentence is not a "yes". Staying completely silent can give the impression that you aren't paying attention, especially on the phone. English speakers do something similar with "uh-huh", "right" and "really?", but あいづち usually come more often, in the small pauses of the speaker's sentences.
culture.try: Watch 2 minutes of an interview or vlog in Japanese and count how many あいづち you hear. Then replay the clip and say はい, ええ or そうですか yourself in the pauses.

checklist: I swap は for も when the predicate repeats, and I never write はも.
I can make any noun sentence negative with じゃないです, and I know じゃありません is the more formal version.
I can answer いいえ with the full negative sentence and then the correct information.
I choose ね (agreement) or よ (new information) based on what the other person already knows.
I read a sentence to the end before deciding whether it's affirmative or negative.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
